Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 90, verses 1–2:

Surah al-Balad

It is Meccan according to the majority, in its entirety. It was also said to be Medinan in its entirety, and it was said to be Medinan except for its first four verses. Both views have been objected to on the grounds that the Exalted's saying, ﴿This city﴾, contradicts them. It is said that because of the strength of this objection, al-Zamakhshari claimed a consensus (ijma') that it is Meccan. It will come, God willing, that some reports contain what clearly indicates that its opening was revealed in Mecca after the Conquest. It has twenty verses, without any disagreement. When, before it, He (glory be to Him) censured those who loved wealth and devoured inheritance greedily, and did not urge the feeding of the needy, He (exalted be He) mentioned here the qualities that are required of the owner of wealth: freeing a neck, and feeding on a day of hunger. Likewise, when He (exalted and majestic be He) mentioned there the soul at peace, He (glory be to Him) mentioned here some of what brings about tranquility. So He, Mighty and Majestic, said:

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿I do not swear by this city﴾. He (glory be to Him) swore by the Sacred City, I mean Mecca, for it is what is meant by "this" by consensus. And what is joined to it: ﴿man was created in toil﴾, immersed in the hardships of struggle and the endurance of difficulties. The Exalted's saying, ﴿And you are a resident (ḥill) in this city﴾, according to what al-Zamakhshari chose in the Kashshaf, is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ) between the oath and its response, and in it is an affirmation of its content by mentioning some of the struggle, in the manner of the excellence of an opening (barā'at al-istihlāl), and an incidental reference (idmāj) to the evil conduct of the polytheists, so that He may explicitly censure them. The meaning of ḥill here is "that which is made lawful" (al-mustaḥall), in the pattern of the passive participle, which is not respected. It is as if it were said: among the struggles is that someone like you, despite the greatness of your sanctity, is made lawful in this sacred city and is not respected, just as game is made lawful outside the Sanctuary. From Shurahbil ibn Sa'd: they forbade themselves to kill game in it and to cut its trees, yet they made lawful your expulsion and your killing. In the emphasis on the human being's being in toil by means of the oath there is a strengthening of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and an incitement to bear that with his noble self, for that is a decreed destiny. It is also permissible that ḥill means ḥalāl, the opposite of ḥarām. Ibn 'Abbas said, in what Ibn Jarir and others transmitted from him: "And you, O Muhammad, it is lawful for you to fight in it, but not for others." Mujahid said: God made it lawful for him (upon him be prayers and peace) for an hour of a day, and He (glory be to Him) said to him: whatever you do in it, you are in lawfulness (ḥill) and will not be held accountable for it. Similar was narrated from Abu Salih, Qatada, 'Atiyya, Ibn Zayd, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak, and its wording: He (glory be to Him) says: "You are lawful in the Sanctuary; kill if you wish, or leave off." That was on the day of the Conquest. On that day the Messenger of God (ﷺ) killed 'Abdullah ibn Khatal, who was the one Quraysh called "the one of two hearts." Abu Barza Sa'id ibn Harb al-Aslami brought him forward, and by the command of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) struck his neck while he was clinging to the curtains of the Ka'ba. He had professed Islam and had written some of the revelation for the Messenger of God (ﷺ), then he apostatized and reviled the Messenger of God (ﷺ), claiming that what he dictated of the Qur'an was from him (upon him be prayers and peace) and not from God. Others were also killed, as is mentioned in the books of biography. Then he (upon him be prayers and peace) said: "Indeed God, may He be exalted, made Mecca sacred on the day He created the heavens and the earth, so it is sacred until the Hour rises. It is not lawful for anyone before me, and it will not be lawful for anyone after me, and it was not made lawful for me except for an hour of a day. Its trees shall not be cut, its grass shall not be pulled up, its game shall not be startled, and its lost property is not lawful to take except by one who announces it." Al-'Abbas said: "O Messenger of God, except idhkhir, for it is for our smiths and our graves and our houses." He (upon him be prayers and peace) said: "Except idhkhir."

The fronting of the predicate-subject (al-musnad ilayhi) here, ḥill, is for restriction (ikhtiṣāṣ), as was indicated in the report of Ibn 'Abbas. And ḥill is in the sense of the future, on the basis that the revelation of the surah was well before the Hijra, which was well before the Conquest. There is a report transmitted by 'Abd ibn Humayd from Ibn Jubayr which clearly indicates that the verse was revealed after Abu Barza struck the neck of Ibn Khatal on the day of the Conquest; if that is sound, it would not be in the sense of the future. But the majority hold the first view. In the exaltation of the sworn-by object and the emphasis of the sworn-to matter by the oath, there is an affirmation of what the discourse is directed toward, namely that the outcome of enduring and struggle is conquest and victory. The purpose is consolation of him (ﷺ). Then its reinforcement is by explicit mention of the coming victory. Exalting the city points to exalting the one who is made lawful in it. In swearing by it there is a preparation for consolation, because exalting the city is among what its people commit of sins, so it is pure and free of them. The meaning of swearing by the city is its exaltation, and in the parenthetical clause is a reinforcement of the exaltation and honor by the fact that one like him (ﷺ), in his lofty rank and the station of prophethood, dwells in it, distinct from what the rabble and the vulgar are upon. The benefit of this is the emphasis of the sworn-to matter, that they are of the sort of natures, so the nobility of place does not benefit them, and the one settled in it. It is as if it were said: I swear by this good city, by itself and by whoever dwells in it, that its people are in a sickness of heart and doubt whose extent cannot be measured. It is also said: ḥill is an adjective, or a verbal noun in the sense of ḥāl. It is said: ḥalla, i.e., alighted, yaḥullu ḥillan and ḥulūlan. It is also said: he is ḥill in such a place, as one says ḥāll bihi. The claim that the adjective from ḥulūl is ḥāll, not ḥill, and that the verbal noun of ḥalla in the sense of alighting is ḥulūl, and that ḥal with a fatha on the ḥa and ḥalal alone, arises from a lack of investigation. The parenthetical clause is for honoring him (ﷺ) by making his alighting the basis for magnifying the city by swearing by it. Some eminent scholars made the clause on this interpretation a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of this city, and likewise some made it circumstantial on both interpretations before, except that the circumstance on the second is concurrent, while on the first it is either anticipated or concurrent if it is said that the descent was at the hour when Mecca was made lawful. Ibn 'Atiyya also made it a circumstantial clause on the first interpretation, namely that ḥill means "one who makes lawful," but he restricted it to the case where lā is a negation and not superfluous, so consider this. Whichever it is, in the demonstrative and in the use of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun there is an exaltation of the city, with both of these.

﴿Wa-walidin﴾ is conjoined to this land by which He swears, and likewise His words ﴿wa-ma walad﴾. The referent of the first is Adam, peace be upon him, and of the second all his offspring, according to what al-Hakim reported and declared sound through the chain of Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas. A group also narrated it from Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Jubayr. It is also said that the referent is Adam, peace be upon him, and the righteous among his descendants. It is said that the referent is Noah, peace be upon him, and his descendants. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu 'Imran that the two are Abraham, peace be upon him, and all his offspring. It is also said that they are Abraham, peace be upon him, and his son Ishmael, peace be upon him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) claimed that it points to that to which it is conjoined, for it is the sanctuary of Abraham, the place where Ishmael grew up, and the birthplace of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), peace be upon them all.

Al-Tabari and al-Mawardi said: It is possible that the "walid" (begetter) is the Prophet (ﷺ), because his mention precedes, and "wa-ma walad" (and what he begot) is his community, based on his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Indeed, I am to you like a father."

There is also the reading of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud): "wa-azwajuhu ummahatuhum wa-huwa abun lahum" ("and his wives are their mothers, and he is a father to them"). In swearing by this there is an exaggeration of his nobility, peace and blessings be upon him, but it is as you see.

It is said that the referent is every begetter and what he begot, among rational and non-rational beings, and this is attributed to Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn Abi Hatim and others reported through the chain of Ikrimah from him that he said: "The walid is the one who begets, and wa-ma walad is the barren one who does not beget, among men and women." This is also attributed to Ibn Jubayr. Here "ma" is a negating particle, so a relative pronoun must be supposed, making the sense intended: "And the begetter, and the one who did not beget." Omitting the relative pronoun in such a construction is not permitted according to the Basran grammarians, and in addition this is contrary to the apparent meaning. Perhaps the apparent sense of the wording is that the two conjoined terms are left unspecified, and the apparent sense of conjoining them to this land is that what is meant is one who has a connection to it and fame through the land's being attributed to him. The most famous in this regard are Abraham and Ishmael, peace be upon them both.

The indefiniteness of "walid," as chosen by more than one commentator, is for glorification. Using "ma" rather than "man," on the basis that "ma walad" means a rational being, is for the sake of describing the attribute, and so it conveys glorification in a context of praise, and that it is something whose true nature cannot be fully grasped because of the intensity of its vagueness. For this reason it conveys amazement or the causing of amazement, even though it is not interrogative, as in His words: ﴿And Allah knows best what she bore﴾, meaning: what a child of great stature she bore. The glorification and amazement, on the supposition that "ma walad" means the offspring of Adam, peace be upon him, for instance, is said to be by way of prevalence (taghlib, the rule of giving precedence to one term over another) and it is said to be by way of abundance. What is specific to humankind among the distinctive qualities of human beings, such as reason and beauty of form, and whoever reflects on human affairs insofar as he is a human being knows that from that standpoint he is magnified and is a cause of wonder.

Indeed, We created man in toil (﴿لَقَدْ خَلَقْنا الإنْسانَ في كَبَدٍ﴾). That is, in exertion and hardship, for he continually endures every kind of hardship from the time the spirit is breathed into him until the time it is taken from him, and what lies beyond that. It is said: كَبِدَ الرَّجُلُ كَبَدًا فَهو أكْبَدُ (kabida al-rajul kabadan fa-huwa akbad), meaning the man's liver (kabid) was afflicted and swelled. The word was then extended in usage until it was applied to every toil and hardship, and from it the word al-mukabadah (persistent struggle against hardship) is derived. It is also said: كَبَتَهُ (kabatahu) meaning "he destroyed him," and its original form is kabadahu, meaning "he struck his liver."

Labid said in elegy for his brother:

O eye, did you weep for Arbad when we rose and the disputants stood in distress?

That is, in the severity of the matter and the difficulty of the calamity.

It is related from Ibn Umar that man struggles to be thankful in ease and struggles to be patient in adversity. It is related from Ibn Abbas, Abdullah ibn Shaddad, Abu Salih, al-Dahhak and Mujahid that they said: that is, We created him upright in stature, standing, and did not make him prone upon his face. Ibn Kaysan said: that is, his head was upright in his mother's womb, and when he was permitted to come out, he turned his head toward his mother's feet. All these sayings are weak and not to be relied upon, unlike the first. Al-Hakim transmitted it and declared it authentic, as did a group, from Ibn Abbas, and it was narrated from more than one of the early generations (al-salaf, the pious predecessors).

Yes, it is permissible that the meaning is: We created him in a severe illness, which is the sickness of the heart and the corruption of the inner self. This is based on the third of the four aspects mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿Nay, I swear by this city﴾ and ﴿while you are a resident of this city﴾. The intended meaning of "man" here is those whom God, when He created them, knew would not believe and would not do righteous deeds. Apparently, in the other interpretations, the intended meaning is the species of man in general. Ibn Zayd said: the intended meaning of "man" is Adam, peace be upon him, and by "kabad" is meant the sky, which is commonly used for the middle of the sky, as in al-kubaydaa, al-kubaydaah and al-kabdaa'. And akbad with a fatha and then a sukun is not correct at all.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 90, verses 5–6:

The pronoun in His saying, ﴿Does he think﴾, according to what is other than that, refers to what the context indicates of what the Prophet, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, endures from the disbelievers of Quraysh, and the violation of the sanctity of the House and of his sanctity, upon him be prayers and peace. Accordingly, the address is to man in general, and the threat is directed at whoever deserves it. It has been said that, taking it as referring to a particular individual, he is Abu al-Ashudd Usayd ibn Kaladah al-Jumahi, who was extremely strong and deceived by his strength. A leather mat from ʿUkaz would be spread out for him, and he would stand upon it and say: "Whoever removes me from it, for him is such-and-such." Ten men would then pull him, and it would tear into pieces while the place of his two feet remained. It has also been said: ʿAmr ibn ʿAbd Wudd; it has been said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah; it has been said: Abu Jahl ibn Hisham; and it has been said: al-Harith ibn ʿAmir ibn Nawfal ibn ʿAbd Manaf. It is permissible that each of these be a cause of revelation, so do not be heedless.

ʿIsam al-Din took the interrogation as expressing amazement, in the sense of: "Does he suppose that no one will have power over him?", meaning power to take revenge on him and to repay him for what he is doing, ﴿anyone﴾, even though he cannot escape the hardship and the enduring of severe trials. The word "an" here is a lightened form of the heavy (an); and perhaps in this there is an incidental implication of disbelief in the Resurrection.

﴿He says: I have squandered wealth in abundance﴾, that is, much, from "talabbada al-shay'" when a thing gathers together. That is, he says this at the time of arrogance, boasting, pride and haughtiness over the believers, and by it he means what he spent for show and reputation. He expressed spending as squandering, to show his indifference and that he did not do this seeking benefit, so it is as if he made the abundant wealth to be wasted. It has also been said: he says this to show the intensity of his enmity toward the Messenger of Allah, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, meaning by the wealth what he spent in opposing him. It has also been said: he says this as harm to him, upon him be prayers and peace. From Muqatil: "al-Harith ibn Nawfal, whenever he committed a sin, would seek a ruling from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, and the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, would command him to make expiation. He said: 'I have squandered wealth in abundance in expiations and dues since I obeyed Muhammad, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace.'" It has also been said: the intended meaning is what was mentioned first, except that this statement is made at the time of retribution against him, which is the Day of Resurrection, and the expression of spending as squandering is because it did not benefit him on that day. Abu Ja'far read "lubbadan" with a doubled ba', and from him and from Zayd ibn ʿAli: "lubdan" with a sukun on the ba'; Mujahid and Ibn Abi al-Zinad read "lubudan" with damma on the lam and the ba'.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 90, verse 7:

﴿Does he think that no one has seen him?﴾ That is: when he was spending what he spent, showing off to people, or out of eagerness to oppose the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The meaning is that God Most High was seeing him, and He, glorified is He, was watching over him. So He, mighty and majestic, will question him about it and recompense him for it.

And in a hadith: "The feet of the servant will not move on the Day of Resurrection until he is questioned about four things: about his life, how he spent it; and about his wealth, from where he gathered it and how he spent it; and about his knowledge, what he did with it."

It is also permissible that the meaning is: "If no one finds him," with the intended sense of "seeing" being "finding" in the sense of necessary existence, and "lam" (لم) being in the meaning of "lan" (لن), and this is expressed with it to affirm that the event will certainly occur. That is, He Most High will find him on the Day of Resurrection and will call him to account for that. And it is reported from al-Kalbi that this speaker was a liar who had not spent anything, so God Most High said: Does he suppose that God did not see whether he did it or did not do it, whether he spent or did not spend? Rather, He, mighty and majestic, saw him and knew from him the opposite of what he claimed.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 90, verses 11–13:

﴿But he has not attempted the steep path.﴾ Al-iqtiham (اقتحام): entering quickly, with force and difficulty. It is said: qahama fi al-amr quhuman, meaning he threw himself into the matter without deliberation.

Al-'Aqabah (العقبة) is a difficult road in a mountain, or in the sea, that is hard to traverse and involves climbing; its plural is 'uqub and 'iqab. Here it is a metaphor for the arduous deeds of high rank before Allah the Exalted, as explained. The indication (qarinah) is evident. Attributing iqtiham to it, with the meaning of doing and earning, is a tarshih (a supporting metaphor). It is also possible that the speaker has made the doing of what was mentioned an iqtiham and a difficult ascent. Mentioning it after "the two highways" makes the metaphor at its highest level of eloquence. The intended meaning is to censure the one spoken of for falling short despite the great blessings and mighty, noble favours Allah the Exalted has bestowed upon him. It is as if it were said: he fell short and did not thank those great blessings and grand favours by doing righteous deeds; rather, he disparaged the blessing, disbelieved the Benefactor, and followed the desire of his soul.

As for the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And what will make you know what the steep path is?﴾ That is: what will inform you of what it is? This is an exaltation of the status of the steep path, which is explained by His words, glorified is He: ﴿The freeing of a neck﴾, and so on. Its explanation by that is based on the claim and metaphor, which there is no doubt is sound, even though the steep path and the freeing are not identical in reality. So there is no need to posit an elided noun, as al-Imam claimed, for the explanation to be valid; that is: "And what will make you know what the attempt at the steep path is? [It is] the freeing... and so on." Some have said: it is possible that the steep path itself is intended to mean gratitude, expressed by it because of its difficulty, and that ﴿And what will make you know﴾ does not contradict this, since it is in the position of "what will make you know what gratitude is: the freeing of a neck." But this, as you see, is far-fetched.

Indeed, I do not hold any of that unless a raised (marfu') narration is sound for it as an explanation of the verse.

Fakk (الفك) is the freeing of one thing from another. The poet said:

*O how many a distressed man I charged to rescue, and a captive whose shackle I unfastened, and he ransomed me.*

It is the verbal noun of fakka, and likewise al-fakak with an open fa', as stated by al-Farra'. The well-known view is that what is meant here is freeing the neck of a slave, by describing the neck with manumission.

Ahmad, Ibn Hibban, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi reported from al-Bara' (may Allah be pleased with him): "A bedouin said: O Messenger of Allah, teach me a deed that will admit me to Paradise. Accordingly, the negation of manumission from the one spoken of is established a fortiori. Al-Raghib said: it is hunger together with fatigue, and it may sometimes be said of thirst together with fatigue. Ibn Abbas interpreted it here as hunger without any qualification. Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibrahim that he said: "On a day when food is scarce." This is not an interpretation according to the meaning it was set for. The description of the day as "of hunger" (dhū masghabah, ذُو مَسْغَبَةٍ) is like what the grammarians say in their phrase: hammun nāṣibun dhū naṣabin (a tiring worry, possessing fatigue), laylun nā'imun dhū nawmin (a sleeping night, possessing sleep), and nahārun ṣā'imun dhū ṣawmin (a fasting day, possessing fasting).

﴿Orphan of near relationship﴾, that is, of kinship. It is also a mimi noun (a noun of place/instance formed with the prefixed mim) from qaruba in the sense of kinship by descent. It is said: "Fulan is dhu qarabati (my kinsman) and dhu maqrabati (my kinsman)," with the same meaning. Al-Zajjaj said: "Fulan qarabati" is ugly, because qarabah is a verbal noun (masdar). He said:

"The stranger weeps over him, though he does not know him, while his own kinsman among the tribe rejoices."

There is a discussion on this point. In the word ﴿feeding﴾ here there is a combination of charity (sadaqah) and maintaining ties of kinship (silah), and both carry the reward that they carry. It is also said that it does not restrict itself to a relative by blood, but includes one who has closeness through neighbourhood.

It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that he explained it here as one who has nothing to shield him from the dust. If this is authentic, it should not be departed from. The waw (in "wa-miskinan") is, according to al-Bahr, for enumeration (tanwi').

The omission of repeating "la" here has been raised as a problem, even though it has entered upon a past verb, and they said: its repetition is necessary in that case, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So he neither affirmed nor prayed﴾, and the saying of al-Hutay'ah:

"And if the favours are among them, they reward them with them; and if they confer favours, they do not spoil them nor do they lament."

And his saying is anomalous:

It has been answered that what is required is its repetition either verbally or in meaning, and here it is repeated in meaning; because explaining "the steep path" by the multiple matters it has been explained by necessarily implies explaining "breaking through" accordingly, so it becomes: "he did not break through the steep path" in the sense of "he did not free a neck and did not feed an orphan..." etc.

It may be said of the verse something similar, namely that the generality in it stands in place of repetition, and it necessarily entails, according to what has been said, the permissibility of: "Zayd and Amr did not come to me," because it means: "Zayd did not come to me and Amr did not come to me." Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' forbade it. It is permissible that it be of this kind.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 90, verse 17–18:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then he became of those who believed﴾. It is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to the negated element, I mean ﴿he did not attempt (iqtaḥama)﴾. It is as if it were said: "So he did not attempt, nor did he believe." It does not follow from this that faith is not included in the concept of the ʿaqabah (the steep path), because it is sufficient for the correctness of the conjunction and the repetition that it is a more noble part which has been singled out by mention through conjunction; thus the form of repetition arises out of necessity, since interpreting it otherwise corrupts the meaning. And it would entail the permissibility of "Zayd did not eat and drank," on the basis of conjunction to the negated element, which the preceding authority prohibits.

It has been said: "lā" here is for supplication (duʿāʾ), and the statement is a supplication against that disbeliever that Allah Exalted not grant him that good. It has also been said: "lā" is a lightened form of "illā" used for urging (taḥḍīḍ), like "hallā" (why not), so it is as if it were said: "Why did he not attempt?" Or the interrogative is elided, and the estimate is: "Then did he not attempt?" This is reported from Ibn Zayd, al-Jubbāʾī and Abū Muslim. In it is the objection that he did not know the lightening of the hortatory alā (ألا التحضيضية), and that, as al-Murtaḍā said, it is ugly to omit the interrogative particle in such a position. The saying of ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿah was criticised for this:

Then they said, "You love her," I said, "Yes, [I love her] in number like the sand, the pebbles and the dust."

And their saying: "If negation were intended, the speech would not be connected to anything, because of the appearance of kāna under the negation and the connection of the speech to it." It is said: the speech is a report about the future, so it is not one in which repetition is necessary; that is: "So he will not attempt the ʿaqabah," because its past is known by observation, so the more important thing is reporting its state in the future, in order that the occurrence be established; he expressed it in the past tense.

al-Ṭībī transmitted from Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī that repeating it (lā) is not obligatory, refuting al-Zajjāj in his claim of that. He said: "It is like lam, and repetition in the manner of ﴿So he neither affirmed nor prayed﴾ does not indicate obligation, as in ﴿They were neither extravagant nor niggardly﴾." And the absence of repetition is evidenced by the saying of Umayyah previously cited:

If You forgive, O Allah, You forgive much, and which of Your servants has not sinned?

What is certain to me is the predominance of repetition; as for its being obligatory, that is not certain. And Allah Exalted knows best.

Ibn Kathīr and the two grammarians (al-Nahwiyyān, i.e. al-Kisāʾī and Ḥamzah) read ﴿fakka﴾ as a past verb, ﴿raqabatan﴾ in the accusative, and ﴿aw aṭʿama﴾ also as a past verb. On this reading, ﴿fakka﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿iqtaḥama﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ). Its meaning is that you did not know the reality of its difficulty for the soul, nor the reality of its reward with Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Abū Rajāʾ read likewise, except that he read ﴿dhā masghabatin﴾ with an alif, on the basis that ﴿dhā﴾ is accusative as object of ﴿aṭʿama﴾; that is: he fed, on one of the days, a person who was in hunger, and ﴿yatīman﴾ would be a substitute for it or an adjective of it. He also, and al-Ḥasan, read ﴿aw iṭʿāmun fī yawmin dhā﴾ with an alif as well, on the basis that it is the object of the verbal noun. Some of the Successors (tābiʿūn) read ﴿fakku raqabatin﴾ with the genitive construction, and ﴿aw aṭʿama﴾ as a past verb, conjoined to the verbal noun, since it is interpreted as such.

The sense of delay understood from ﴿thumma﴾ in His saying ﴿Then he became﴾ etc. is hierarchical (rutbī), so faith is above all that preceded it, because it independently constitutes a cause of salvation and gratitude without deeds, as in the case of one who believed under its condition and died on that same day before any deed became obligatory upon him; that benefits him and saves him, unlike anything else, which is not counted without it. His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿And enjoined one another to patience﴾ is conjoined to "believed"; that is: some of them enjoined others to patience in faith and steadfastness upon it, or to that and patience in acts of obedience, or to it, and patience in sins and in the trials by which a person is tested.

﴿And enjoined one another to compassion﴾, that is: to mercy toward His servants, Mighty and Majestic, and among that is commanding the good and forbidding the evil; or they enjoined one another with the causes of Allah's mercy and the good deeds that lead to it, with "compassion" being a metaphor for its cause, or the speech is on the assumption of an omitted genitive. It is mentioned that ﴿And enjoined one another to patience﴾ points to the magnification of the command of Allah Exalted, and ﴿And enjoined one another to compassion﴾ points to tenderness toward the creation of Allah Exalted; these are two foundations upon which the obedience revolves. This is what some of the verifiers (muḥaqqiqīn) said: the principle in Sufism is two things: sincerity with the Truth, and good character with the creation.

﴿Those﴾ is an indication of the relative (mawṣūl) in respect of its being characterised by what is within its relative clause, and what is in it of the sense of distance together with the nearness of the one indicated, for what has passed many times; that is: those who are described by the noble attributes mentioned. ﴿The companions of the right hand﴾, that is: the direction of the right, in which are the happy ones, or [the word derives from] "blessing" (al-yumn), because they are blessed upon themselves and upon others.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 90, verses 19–20:

﴿And those who disbelieve in Our signs﴾ — that is, in what We have set up as a proof of the truth, from a book and a proof, or [in] the Qur'an.

﴿They are the companions of the left hand﴾ — that is, the direction of the left, in which are the wretched; or [it refers to] the ill omen upon themselves and upon others.

﴿Over them is a fire﴾ — great — ﴿closed in﴾, sealed shut, from āṣadtu (I closed) the door when one shuts and seals it. This is the dialect of Quraysh, according to what is narrated from Mujahid. The apparent sense of Ibn 'Abbas's words is that it is not restricted to them. Among examples of this is the poet's saying:

"My she-camel yearns for the mountains of Mecca, and between her and them are the gates of San'a, sealed."

It is also possible that it is from ūṣidat (it was closed), meaning "shut" as well, and it was made with a hamza in the manner of one who reads al-su'q with a hamza; and more than one of the Seven read mūṣadatun without a hamza. It appears therefore that it is from ūṣidat. It is also said that it may be from āṣadtu, with the hamza softened. The poet said:

"A people whose sons treat lice, and smooth chains, and a door sealed."

The meaning is that its doors are locked, and they were locked only to intensify the punishment — and we seek refuge with God Almighty — upon them. He explicitly stated their threat but did not explicitly state the promise for the believers, because this is more fitting to what the discourse is directed at, and more suitable to the aim and purpose. For this reason the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl) was brought with them, to convey restriction (al-ḥaṣr), and they were regarded as absent, as though they were in no way fit to be pointed to. That course was not taken in general in the first sentence, which concerns the believers.

It is related from al-Shimni that he said: The wisdom in leaving out the pronoun of separation in the first two and bringing in place of it the demonstrative is that the demonstrative is used to distinguish what is meant in the most complete distinction, as in his saying:

"This is Abu al-Saqr, unique in his virtues, of the lineage of Shayban, between al-Dal and al-Sullam."

The pronoun does not do this. The distant demonstrative conveys glorification, by placing the elevated status of what is pointed to at a rank beyond its degree. So the demonstrative is for glorification, and the pointing is to their distinction and their deserving the utmost fame, unlike the companions of the left hand; the pronoun does not convey that. End of quotation.

In this there is the point that the demonstrative, just as it conveys glorification, also conveys contempt, as in His saying, exalted be He: ﴿So that is the one who repulses the orphan﴾. And the utmost fame, just as it occurs in good, occurs in evil too. So what prevents considering their deserving the utmost fame in evil? In sum, what he mentioned is of no weight, and what we have mentioned is likely the better, so reflect.
